body.text: When Melbourne’s Tullamarine Airport opened in 1970 air travellers welcomed it as a marvel of modern efficiency. With its easy drop-off and pick-up areas and swish new baggage carousels it made the other capital city airports look old-fashioned, and they were.

Tullamarine’s greenfields site meant it could combine domestic and international terminals in the one grand structure, providing a seamless travel experience, especially for overseas arrivals whose final destination lay beyond Melbourne. Other capital cities struggled with their remnant airports, which — like Melbourne’s superseded Essendon, Sydney’s Mascot, Brisbane’s Eagle Farm and most other capital city airports — were on very constrained sites. With ever-bigger jets required much longer runways and passenger numbers growing rapidly, those constrained airports ended up separating domestic and international arrivals when they came to build new terminals, and some had to run tedious bus services between terminals.

Arun Chandu and Matt Harvey’s Melbourne Airport Tullamarine: A History is a hymn of praise to both Tullamarine Airport and the aviation industry. The authors — Chandu a medico who did a PhD on the planning history of Tullamarine, Harvey an academic lawyer who lives under the Essendon flight path — have researched a wide range of sources and unearthed many evocative illustrations.

Chandu and Harvey explain how airports are a federal government responsibility under the Australian Constitution, so the Commonwealth acquired the land they were to be built on in much the same way as it acquired land for quarantine stations and defence purposes. They pay tribute to the work of Bill Bradfield, a senior official in the Department of Civil Aviation. Born in 1910, the youngest child of J.J.C. Bradfield of Harbour Bridge fame, Bill gained a doctorate in Engineering from Oxford and became fascinated by aerodrome design. By the late 1940s his responsibilities included all airports and ground facilities in Australia. He recognised the importance of the Commonwealth acquiring land around an airport’s periphery to prevent new housing estates being built too close to runways.

The noise issue continues to plague airports worldwide, not least in Sydney, where the airport must keep to a strict curfew. Thanks to Bradfield, Tullamarine had ample buffer land. It was always conceived as a twenty-four-hour airport, as is the new Western Sydney Airport. No one at the time imagined that northwestern Melbourne would be engulfed by the huge suburban housing estates that surround the airport today.

In the postwar world, with comparatively low air traffic volumes, Bradfield hoped an airport would be sufficiently attractive for the non-travelling public to visit it, especially if it had restaurants, open-air cafes and public galleries. He thought airports would need the extra revenue because landing fees, hangar rentals and other ground charges wouldn’t cover their operating costs. Even as late as the 1960s Heathrow airport imagined itself as “a glamourous enclave of global travel isolated from the workday world.” If you have had the misfortune to land at Heathrow anytime in recent decades it is a chaotic experience most passengers regret, the only consolation being the Heathrow Express, which will get you to the centre of London in fifteen minutes.

All Australian airports provide car parks, none bigger than Tullamarine. Along with car rental concessions, they have become quite a money spinner. Taxis and now Uber remain expensive for departures and arrivals at Tullamarine, and it is still common practice to expect friends or relatives to pick you up or drop you off. The elevated roadway for departures is now beset by endless traffic jams, and at peak times staff have to be rostered onto the pedestrian crossings to prevent mass carnage. Neverending road works at Tullamarine keep drivers on their toes, while rent-a-car customers enter and exit the airport at their peril.

In the days before airports were leased out to private corporations and the federal government still owned airlines (TAA and Qantas), airports were seen as a public facility and a vital link across Australia’s vast distances. The staggering growth in air travel, especially with larger jets, created huge income streams for both the airport corporations and the airlines. TAA and Ansett promoted mass tourism into Queensland, where both airlines developed their own tourist resorts that looked particularly enticing from a wintry Melbourne. With the demise of the two-airline agreement (TAA and Ansett), the bankruptcy of Ansett and the entry of new airlines including Virgin (now part-owned by Qatar) and Jetstar (Qantas subsidiary), airfares became more affordable, especially with competition from new international players.

As Joe Aston shows in The Chairman’s Lounge (2024), airport lounges have become political lobbying tools, enabling Qantas to curry favour with politicians and business leaders. High flyers, wealthy business people and senior public servants happily avoid mixing with the general public. If they are not sufficiently influential to get an invitation to the Chairman’s Lounge they can fall back on the lounges that Qantas and Virgin (taking over the original Ansett lounges) offer to frequent flyers.

The human face of the airport has also changed irrevocably. We still have real pilots and real cabin staff, but self-check-in means that if you have a problem you have to master the machine and the app. This book, especially its pre-2000 illustrations, is a reminder of the lost world before security scanning became mandatory in 2004. It has very little to say about the unpleasant aspects of air travel, including the advent of mass tourism.

Modern airports are nothing like the airport city Bill Bradfield imagined. They are giant transit sites where the well-heeled are well treated and the economy passengers board last. While Australians still cling to residual notions of egalitarianism in the air, wealthier travellers head for business class, and the cheaper economy seats are a real squeeze.

Forty-two airlines now operate into and out of Tullamarine, with 305 takeoffs and landings each day and thirty-five million passengers each year. Most airlines now include an acknowledgement, on descending, of prior Indigenous occupation, but apart from some tacky souvenirs in airport shops there is little in the airport itself to help passengers understand what that really means.

The authors show just how much planning goes into runway design and the amount of money spent on terminals, especially now that most passengers no longer walk on the tarmac. As they regretfully explain, Tullamarine remains cursed by the failure of both the airport management and the state government to create a rail link to the city centre and the rest of the suburban rail and tram network.

But they are too coy about the failure of the Liberal governments of Henry Bolte and particularly Jeff Kennett to build the rail link, nor do they admit to the failure of successive corporate owners, mainly superannuation firms and fund managers, to make that happen. Sydney (under pressure of the 2000 Olympics), Brisbane and even Perth now offer a rail link, but a single accident on the so-called Tullamarine Freeway can cause thousands of passengers to miss their flights, including those booked on the Skybus network. The authors are also remarkably coy about climate change concerns, almost as if it didn’t exist, even though airlines increasingly offer travellers, at a cost, an opportunity to assuage their guilt.

Reasonably priced at $49.99, Melbourne Airport Tullamarine: A History, will appeal to aviation aficionados and regular flyers, and is salutary reading for anyone who lives under a flight path. Engagingly written, the book has an intense double-column text setting, which is not easy on the eye. In the era of privatised airport corporations and powerful airlines is it a timely reminder that federal government oversight of airport planning, and especially the noise implications of extra runways and the necessity to acquire more land for buffer zones, remains vital so the nearby citizenry can sleep at night. •
